name: West Face

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Darrington, drive SR 530 north about 8 miles to the Suiattle River Road (FS Road 26) and follow it east about 20 miles to the Downey Creek Trailhead at about 1,450 feet, just past the Downey Creek bridge; the trail leaves the north side of the road and parking is on the south side. A Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass is required. The Suiattle River Road is prone to washout closures, so check its status first.

waypoints.name: North Peak Summit
waypoints.directions: From the col, make a descending traverse across the Chikamin Glacier, watching for crevasses and crossing the bergschrund on a snow bridge, to the foot of the West Face. Scramble along the ramp beneath the left side of the face to where it splits; the route starts just past the split at a small cairn. Climb five pitches to the terminal terrace, then move right along the terrace to a chimney that leads to the summit.

approach_variants.name: Downey Creek, Itswoot Ridge and the Dome-Chikamin col
approach_variants.notes: This is a two-day approach each way and there is no short way in. From the Downey Creek Trailhead follow the valley trail to the Bachelor Creek crossing, then the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path through heavy brush to Cub Lake and Itswoot Ridge for the first camp. From there continue over the ridge and glacier ground to the Dome-Chikamin col and make a high camp. On the climbing day, cross the Chikamin Glacier from the col to the foot of the wall.
approach_variants.season: Midsummer to early autumn; the glacier crossing opens up as the season goes on and later parties have reached the ice by the rock rib coming down off the neighbouring summit instead
hazards: Big crevasses on the Chikamin Glacier; the bergschrund is crossed on a snow bridge and is a place to move quickly
Heavy bushwhacking on the Bachelor Creek path
Sustained hard free climbing on a very steep face, two days from the car in either direction
approach_variants.baseFinding: Cross the glacier from the col to the foot of the face and then stop looking at the wall — the start is not reached from the ice. Get onto the ramp that runs beneath the left side of the face and scramble along it. The ramp splits, and the route starts just past that split, with a small cairn on the ground marking it. Those two things together, the split in the ramp and the cairn beside it, are the proof; either on its own is not enough on a face this size. From there the first climbing goes up a shallow corner on thin cracks, flakes and occasional knobs on clean white granite, and the objective is the centre of the wall. If you are still on the glacier below a uniformly steep face with no ramp beneath you, you have not gained the access ledge. If the ramp is running on unbroken with no branch in it, keep going — you are short of the start.

itinerary: Day 1: Hike Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails to Cub Lake basin / Dome-Chickamin col area and make camp (long day with significant brush and blowdown on Bachelor Creek). Day 2: Cross Chickamin Glacier to the base of the West Face, climb the route (5-6 pitches), rappel the descent, return to camp. Day 3: Hike out via Bachelor/Downey Creek trails.
descent_text: Rappel down the center of the West Face via four consecutive double-rope rappels of roughly 50 m, 50 m, 50 m and 20 m, using natural anchor features and existing bolt/gear anchors established on the granite. Ensure proper rope management to avoid tangling on the steep granite face. Once back at the base of the route, climb back up to the Chikamin-Dome Col via the Chickamin Glacier approach, watching carefully for crevasses and potential moat crossings. From the col, descend the cross-country route back to Bachelor Flats (taking approximately 8-10 hours depending on snow coverage and conditions). From Bachelor Flats, follow the Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead (6-8 hours depending on fitness and pack weight). Total descent time from summit to vehicle is typically 3-4 days.
pro_tips: Start early from the high camp to maximize daylight and avoid afternoon thunderstorms
Pitch 2 contains the technical and psychological crux; focus and confidence critical
The approach requires serious glacier travel skills; crevasse rescue knowledge mandatory
Carry minimal water on the climb itself as it adds weight during sustained steep climbing
Plan for a 2-3 day approach and 3-4 day descent; rushing this objective has led to accidents
July offers the most stable weather window; plan accordingly
The onsight FFA demonstrates clean rock and reliable protection; trust the granite
